key_insight: The paper shows that governing ODEs can be uniquely identified from solution trajectories only when the induced Hausdorff distance between candidate solution sets is sufficiently separated, yielding quantitative identifiability and sample-complexity bounds.
engineering_relevance: This provides a theoretical foundation for scientific machine learning systems that recover dynamics from data, helping designers know when equation discovery is possible, stable, and data-efficient.
method: Define a Hausdorff-distance metric on sets of ODE solutions to compare equations by worst-case trajectory mismatch.
Derive identifiability bounds for linear ODEs and nonlinear ODEs with Lipschitz/Hölder vector fields.
Use metric entropy estimates to obtain sample-complexity bounds for recovering the governing equation from multiple observations.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis across broad ODE classes, including identifiability characterization and metric-entropy-based sample-complexity estimates, rather than empirical experiments.
watch_item: The guarantees depend on observing sufficiently rich solution data over admissible initial conditions, so real-world performance may degrade under sparse, noisy, or incomplete trajectories.
paper_title: Recovering Governing Equations from Solution Data: Identifiability Bounds for Linear and Nonlinear ODEs
